core: Working definition of cellular injury: damage to cells that disrupts normal function
Five common causes: lack of oxygen, toxins, infection, trauma, heat and cold
Apoptosis (programmed cell death) versus necrosis (accidental cell death that triggers inflammation)
What injured cells do: swell, change, release signals
The body's response: inflammation as the standard initial response, then repair and regeneration
Clinical significance: injury patterns explain symptoms
supporting: Cell death endpoint defined as death of living tissues (NCI)
Regeneration as replacement by new cells of the same type
Inflammation limiting injury extent, blunting the cause, and initiating repair
outOfScope: Detailed molecular pathways of apoptosis (caspases, mitochondrial pathways)
Specific morphological types of necrosis (coagulative, liquefactive, caseous)
Free radical and reperfusion injury mechanisms

claims.claim: A working definition of cellular injury is damage to cells that disrupts their normal function; injury forms a spectrum from reversible stress to cell death.

Apoptosis is a type of cell death in which a series of molecular steps within a cell lead to its death; it is one method the body uses to get rid of unneeded or abnormal cells and is also called programmed cell death.
Necrosis refers to the death of living tissues.
Necrosis is accidental cell death that causes inflammation, whereas apoptosis is programmed cell death that does not cause inflammation.
Inflammation is the standard initial response to injury: it limits the extent of the injury, eliminates or blunts the cause of the injury, and initiates repair and regeneration of the damaged tissue.
Regeneration is the process by which injured tissue is replaced by new cells of the same type.
Common causes of cellular injury include lack of oxygen, toxins, infections, trauma, and excessive heat or cold.

positions: Classic textbook teaching (OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, section 4.6): necrosis causes inflammation; apoptosis does not.
More advanced sources note that massive or dysregulated apoptosis can provoke some inflammatory response as dying cells are cleared.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the standard textbook distinction — apoptosis is orderly and non-inflammatory, necrosis is accidental and inflammatory — and keeps the nuance out of scope for a foundations lesson. The question bank and clinical examples consistently follow the textbook distinction.

unsupportedExistingClaims: Generated-draft claims about specific intracellular mechanisms and morphological subtypes of necrosis were discarded: the verified source set does not support them at the detail the draft attempted.
Draft wording that presented inflammation as a disease rather than a response to injury was replaced with the source-supported framing that inflammation is the standard initial response to injury.
correctionsNeeded: Full rewrite of the generated draft: original prose grounded in the four verified sources.
Working definition of cellular injury attributed and anchored to the tissue-injury framing of OpenStax A&P 2e section 4.6, with the NCI necrosis entry marking the cell-death endpoint.
Five causes (lack of oxygen, toxins, infection, trauma, heat and cold) each given one line with an original example, per the source list of causes.
Reversible-versus-irreversible framing adopted as the central organizing distinction.
Apoptosis defined per the NCI dictionary and corroborated by Alberts et al.; necrosis defined per the NCI dictionary with the inflammation consequence per OpenStax.
Clinical application section rewritten around the injury-pattern-explains-symptoms idea with an original heart-attack example.
